summary: Allows Anycast-RP to be used inside a domain that runs only PIM. Other multicast protocols, such as MSDP, which has traditionally solved this problem, are not required. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: PIM needs a rendezvous point, a router that keeps track of which sources are sending to a multicast group. Normally one router does that job. This RFC lets several routers share the job, using the same IP address, so that a failure of one does not stop the multicast traffic. It removes the need for MSDP inside a single domain.

questions: how does anycast rp work with pim
do i need msdp for anycast rp
what is a pim register message
subtitle: Letting several routers share one multicast rendezvous point address, without needing MSDP inside the domain.

tldr.problem: In PIM sparse mode, one rendezvous point keeps the state of a multicast group. If that router fails, the group stops working, and sharing the job between routers has traditionally needed MSDP, which is complex.
tldr.mechanism: Several routers are configured with the same rendezvous point address on their loopback interfaces, and each knows the addresses of the others. A router that receives a PIM Register from a designated router copies it to every other router in the set and stops the designated router from registering again.
tldr.outcome: Sources anywhere in the domain reach all receivers, whatever rendezvous point they joined, and the failure of one rendezvous point is repaired as fast as unicast routing converges. The RFC also states the security limits: forged Registers can still cause a denial of service.

facts.label: When a Register is copied
facts.value: Only when it was received from an address not in the Anycast-RP list

facts.label: Copies sent
facts.value: One to each other RP in the Anycast-RP set, with the sending RP's own address as the source

facts.label: TTL handling
facts.value: The TTL of the original Register is copied to the copies

facts.label: Address used for the set
facts.value: A separate IP address, distinct from the addresses the RPs use to talk to each other

facts.label: MSDP
facts.value: Still needed to advertise internal sources outside the domain and to learn external sources

facts.label: Mixed deployment
facts.value: An RP without support may have receivers joined but should not have sources registering to it

today: RFC 4610 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the description of Anycast-RP inside a PIM-only domain.

sections.title: What the Operator Has to Configure
sections.content:
A unicast IP address is chosen to use as the RP address. This address is statically configured, or distributed using a dynamic protocol, to all PIM routers throughout the domain. A set of routers in the domain is then chosen to act as RPs for this RP address, and these routers are called the Anycast-RP set.

Each router in the Anycast-RP set is configured with a loopback interface using the RP address, and each router also needs a separate IP address to be used for communication between the RPs. The RP address, or a prefix that covers the RP address, is injected into the unicast routing system inside the domain, so that traffic addressed to it reaches the nearest of the set.

Each router in the Anycast-RP set is configured with the addresses of all the other routers in the set. This must be consistently configured in all RPs in the set. The address used for the RP address in the domain, the Anycast-RP address, needs to be different from the addresses the routers use to communicate with each other.

The appendix gives a possible configuration command, ip pim anycast-rp <anycast-rp-addr> <rp-addr>, where the first address describes the Anycast-RP set that the first-hop and last-hop PIM routers register and join to, and the second is the address where copies of Register messages are sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator picks one IP address to act as the rendezvous point address and either configures it everywhere by hand or distributes it with a dynamic protocol. Several routers are chosen to act as rendezvous points for that address, and each of them is configured with that address on a loopback interface. Each also needs a second, separate address, used only for talking to the other rendezvous points. The address, or a prefix that covers it, is injected into the unicast routing system, so traffic sent to it lands on the nearest of them. Every router in the set is configured with the addresses of all the others, and the configuration must be the same in all of them.

sections.title: How a Source Gets Registered
sections.content:
The RFC works through a domain with three RPs, where receivers join the closest RP according to where unicast routing metrics take them, and two sources send packets to their respective RPs. RP1, RP2 and RP3 are all assigned the same IP address, which is used as the Anycast-RP address, RPA.

The procedure when S1 starts sourcing traffic runs as follows. S1 sends a multicast packet, and the designated router directly attached to S1 forms a PIM Register message to send to the Anycast-RP address. The unicast routing system delivers the Register to the nearest RP, in this case RP1. RP1 receives it, decapsulates it and sends the packet down the shared tree to reach the receivers R1 and R1'.

RP1 is configured with the IP addresses of RP2 and RP3. Since the Register message did not come from one of the RPs in the Anycast-RP set, RP1 assumes the packet came from a designated router. If the Register is not addressed to the Anycast-RP address, an error has occurred and it should be rate-limited and logged. RP1 then sends a copy of the Register message from S1's designated router to both RP2 and RP3, using its own IP address as the source address. RP1 MAY join back to the source tree by triggering an (S1,G) Join towards S1, but it MUST create (S1,G) state. RP1 then sends a Register-Stop back to the designated router.

RP2 receives the Register from RP1, decapsulates it and also sends the packet down the shared tree to reach receiver R2. RP2 sends a Register-Stop back to RP1, and MAY wait to send it if it decides to join the source tree, in which case the Register-Stop is sent when the next Register is received. RP3 receives the Register, decapsulates it, and since no receivers are joined for the group it can discard the packet; it still sends a Register-Stop back and creates (S1,G) state so that it can join quickly if a receiver appears later. RP1 processes the Register-Stop from each of RP2 and RP3, and takes no specific action.

The procedure for S3 sending is the same, but RP3 sends the copy of the Register to RP1 and RP2. This shows how sources anywhere in the domain, associated with different RPs, can reach all receivers, also associated with different RPs, in the same domain.
sections.plainLanguage: When a source starts sending, the designated router next to it builds a PIM Register message and sends it to the shared rendezvous point address. The unicast routing system delivers it to the nearest rendezvous point, which is the one that will forward the traffic down the shared tree. That router forwards the packets down the tree, and then sends a copy of the Register to every other rendezvous point in the set, using its own address as the source, and stops the designated router from registering again. Each of the other rendezvous points does the same forwarding down its own tree and sends a Register-Stop back. A rendezvous point that receives a Register from another rendezvous point does not forward it again, so the copies do not multiply.

sections.title: Guidelines for Implementers
sections.content:
An RP sends a copy of a Register only if the Register is received from an IP address not in the Anycast-RP list, that is, if it came from a designated router and not from another RP. An implementation MUST safeguard against inconsistently configured Anycast-RP sets in each RP by copying the Time to Live of a Register message to the Register messages it copies and sends to the other RPs.

Each designated router that registers a source sends the message to the Anycast-RP address, which results in the packet getting to the closest physical RP, so there are no changes to the designated router logic. Packets flow to all receivers no matter what RP they have joined to. The source is registered to a single RP by the designated router, and it is the responsibility of the RP that receives the PIM Register from the designated router, the closest RP based on routing metrics, to get the packet to all other RPs in the set.

Logic is changed only in the RPs, and the change is for sending copies of Register messages. Register-Stop processing is unchanged, although an implementation MAY suppress sending Register-Stop messages in response to a Register received from an RP. The rate-limiting of Register and Register-Stop messages is done end to end, from the designated router to the first RP and on to the others, so no specific rate-limiting logic is needed between the RPs.

When topology changes occur, the existing source tree and the existing shared trees adjust as they do today according to PIM-SM. Physical RP changes are as fast as unicast route convergence. An RP that does not support this specification can be mixed with RPs that do, but the non-supporter should not have sources registering to it, though it may have receivers joined to it. If Null Registers are sent, that is, Registers with an IP header and no IP payload, they MUST be replicated to all of the RPs in the set so that source state remains alive for active sources. The number of RPs in the set should remain small so that the amount of non-native replication is kept to a minimum. Because the RP that receives a Register from the designated router sends the copies at the same time as it sends the Register-Stop to the designated router, there could be packet loss and lost state in the other RPs until the designated router sends Register messages again.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the rendezvous points change: the designated router logic is untouched, and the processing of Register-Stop messages is unchanged. Each copy of a Register carries the same TTL as the original, so an inconsistently configured set cannot loop the message around. The number of rendezvous points should stay small, because every extra one adds copies of the traffic that is not native to it. If a copy is lost, the state at the other end is recovered the next time the designated router registers again.

sections.title: The Remaining Role of MSDP
sections.content:
The objective of this Anycast-PIM proposal is to remove the dependence on using MSDP, which can be achieved by removing MSDP peering between the Anycast-RPs. However, to advertise internal sources to routers outside of a PIM routing domain and to learn external sources from other routing domains, MSDP may still be required.

In a stub domain, when there are internal sources that need to be advertised externally, an Anycast-RP that receives a Register message, either from a designated router or from another Anycast-RP, processes it as described in this specification as well as as described in PIM-SM. That means a Source-Active for the same internal source could be originated by multiple Anycast-RPs doing the MSDP peering. There is nothing inherently wrong with this other than the source being advertised into the MSDP infrastructure from multiple places, and configuration of one or more rather than all Anycast-RP MSDP routers would allow only those routers to originate SAs for the internal source.

For learning sources external to a domain, the MSDP SA messages could arrive at multiple MSDP-peering Anycast-RPs and the rules for processing an SA should be followed. If G is joined in the domain, an (S,G) join is sent towards the source, and if data accompanies the SA, each Anycast-PIM RP doing MSDP peering forwards the data down each of its respective shared trees. If not every Anycast-RP has external MSDP peering connections, the ones that do follow the same procedure as if a Data-Register or Null-Register was received, and send Registers to the other members of the set. To avoid this periodic control traffic, it is recommended that all Anycast-RPs be configured with external MSDP peering sessions. Within a transit domain, it is recommended that an Anycast-RP set should not be mixed with MSDP peering among the members.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the proposal is to remove the need for MSDP between the rendezvous points in one domain. MSDP may still be needed to advertise internal sources outside the domain and to learn about external sources. When a rendezvous point with MSDP peering receives a Register, the same copy is sent to the other members of the set, so that every member has the source state.

sections.title: Security Consideration
sections.content:
An attacker may forge a Register message using one of the addresses in the Anycast-RP list in order to overwhelm the target RP in a denial-of-service attack, to inject unauthorized data to receivers served by the RP, or to inject unauthorized data and create bogus SA entries in other PIM domains if the target RP has external MSDP peerings. An attacker may also forge a Register-Stop message using one of the addresses in the list, but besides denial of service the effect is limited, because an RP usually ignores Register-Stop messages.

The denial-of-service attack using forged Register or Register-Stop messages cannot be prevented, but the RP can still be protected, for example by rate-limiting incoming messages or by refusing to process any Register-Stop messages. The actual protection mechanism is implementation specific.

The distribution of unauthorized data and bogus Register messages can be prevented using the method described in PIM-SM. When RP1 sends a copy of a Register to RP2, RP1 acts as PIM-SM describes the designated router and RP2 acts as PIM-SM describes the RP. An RP can be configured with a unique Security Association and Security Parameters Index for traffic to each member of the Anycast-RP set, but that results in a key management problem, so it may be preferable in PIM domains where all RPs are under a single administrative control to use the same authentication algorithm parameters, including the key, for all Register packets in a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker could forge a Register message using an address from the rendezvous point list. That could flood the target router, inject data to receivers, or create bogus source entries in other domains through MSDP. A denial-of-service attack cannot be prevented, but the router can rate-limit incoming messages and refuse to process Register-Stop messages. The copies sent between rendezvous points can be protected with the PIM authentication method, where the sending router takes the role of the designated router and the receiving one the role of the rendezvous point.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT KEEP THE SET WORKING

items.title: Copy only from a designated router
items.text: A Register is copied to the other RPs only when it arrives from an address outside the Anycast-RP list.

items.title: Copy the TTL
items.text: Each copy keeps the TTL of the original, so an inconsistently configured set cannot loop it.

items.title: Keep the set small
items.text: Every extra RP means more replication of traffic that is not native to it.

items.title: Replicate Null Registers
items.text: Registers with no payload must be copied to every RP, so that source state stays alive.
